li.font: In Java 7, an interface was considered as pure abstraction which was designed only to represent a contract. It could contain only abstract methods, i.e., methods without implementation.
Any concrete class implementing that interface must provide implementation for every abstract method.

If a class doesn't provide implementation for all the abstract methods, it must be declared as an abstract class. Such an abstract class can leave the remaining methods unimplemented, but eventually, the first concrete subclass must implement all of them.

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 818px; height: 1px; padding-top: 458px; margin-left: 428px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: left; color: #000000;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Georgia; color: #000000; line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

li.font: Java 8 introduced the default keyword which allowed an interface to contain methods with implementation.
An implementing class is not required to override a default method. It can either use the default implementation provided by the interface or override it with its own implementation.

The main purpose of introducing default methods was backward compatibility. Earlier, adding a new abstract method to an existing interface forced every implementing class to implement it, otherwise the code would not compile.
With default methods, a new method can be added to an existing interface without breaking existing implementations, because the interface itself provides a default implementation.

p.font: A default method is optional for the implementing class, not for the interface. The method already exists in the interface with its implementation.

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 818px; height: 1px; padding-top: 864px; margin-left: 428px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: left; color: #000000;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Georgia; color: #000000; line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

li.font: Before Java 8, common helper logic was usually placed in a separate utility class (e.g., PaymentUtil, MathUtil, ValidationUtil).
with Java 8, such utility methods replaced with static method which is written inside interface itself.
A static method belongs to the interface itself, not to its implementing classes.
It must be called using the interface name, i.e., InterfaceName.methodName().
Static methods are not inherited by implementing classes, so they cannot be overridden.

p.font: If multiple static methods inside the same interface need the same common logic (e.g., validation, logging, or database connection setup), that logic has to be duplicated because Java 8 doesn't allow private methods inside interfaces.

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 818px; height: 1px; padding-top: 1239px; margin-left: 426px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: left; color: #000000;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Georgia; color: #000000; line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

li.font: Java 9 introduced private methods inside interface which can be of two types: private instance methods and Private static method.

A private method can be called only from within the same interface. if it is a private instance method then it can be called only from default methods whereas a private static method can be called from both - default methods and static methods.
The main purpose of a private method is to extract common logic shared by multiple default methods, and multiple static methods which helps in removing code duplication and improve maintainability.
